newsitem.title: UK: Al-Fayed courts Establishment but still no passport. [CORRECTED 14:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Al-Fayed courts Establishment but still no passport. [CORRECTED 14:40 GMT]

text.p: Britain refuses to give Egyptian-born tycoon Mohamed Al Fayed the passport he covets. Now he could be father-in-law to Princess Diana.

"We might, just might, look to the future of this country's Establishment and wonder if Al Fayed has forced the Establishment moat and is knocking at the Castle gates," The Guardian said as his son Dodi courted Diana.
The outsider, once labelled "The Hero from Zero" by arch business rival Tiny Rowland, could end up the insider.
The royalty-obsessed tabloids have plunged into a frenzy of speculation about the House of Harrods enjoying a love match with the House of Windsor.
"They have my blessing," Al Fayed said of the couple whose blurrily photographed holiday clinches have been pored over with fascination by the nation.

"I don't know what their plans are for the future but as long as they both remain happy, that warms my heart," said the man asked by Diana's father, Earl Spencer, to "keep an eye on the family" before he died.
The contrast between how France and Britain treats the owner of the "Top People" store Harrods could not be sharper.
He returned the Paris Ritz hotel to its former glory and restored the Paris villa where the Duke and Duchess of Windsor lived after he abdicated as king.
France gave Al Fayed the Legion D'Honneur and President Jacques Chirac was fulsome in praise of the tycoon.

After probing the take-over of Harrods, Britain's department of trade and industry concluded in its report: "The Fayeds dishonestly represented their origins, their wealth, their business interests and their resources."

His application to become a British citizen was turned down with Al Fayed complaining bitterly that he had lived blamelessly in Britain for 30 years, employed 6,000 people and contributed millions of pounds in tax.
Al Fayed then triggered a sleaze scandal that helped to bring down the Conservative government when he revealed he had given cash to members to ask (corrects from "answer") questions in parliament.
Diana sparked controversy when she and her two sons went on holiday with Al Fayed in his luxury yacht.
Then came the liaison with his film-producer son that could give the family the kind of social entree that Jackie Kennedy supplied Aristotle Onassis when she married the Greek shipping magnate.

Al Fayed, resplendent in elegant double-breasted suits, is equally at ease standing beside Queen Elizabeth at the Royal Windsor Horse show or cheering for West London's Fulham Football Ground where he became its major shareholder.

The ubiquitous owner of the world's most famous department store boasts royal warrants from Queen Elizabeth, Prince Philip, the Queen Mother and Prince Charles who have all given their seal of approval to Harrods.
Philip has lunched at Harrods, Al Fayed has sponsored the Grand Prix at the Royal Windsor Horse Show. He backs the charities closest to Diana's heart.
A Sunday Telegraph profile of the flamboyant magnate once used the phrase "profoundly Levantine" to describe him.

"At base, though, he is still the trader from Alexandria and his billions and fabulous possessions ...have done little to add polish to his manner or indeed anything to his standing in British society," it said.

Al Fayed is famed for his tenacity in business. If his son woos and wins one of the world's most famous and glamorous women, then the leaders of British High Society may at last welcome him into their rarefied ranks.
